purpose: Approved Marrow ED8 Biochemistry Chapter 11 explanation rollout. Raw imported source remains immutable; this file contains learner-facing augmentation only.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH11_Q001.takeaway: The urea cycle spans both mitochondria and cytoplasm.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH11_Q001.displayText:
The urea cycle, also called the ornithine or Krebs–Henseleit cycle, is divided between mitochondria and cytoplasm. Its first reactions occur in mitochondria, while later reactions proceed in the cytosol.

This compartmentalization is a high-yield feature of the pathway.

rationales.a: The urea cycle is not confined to the cytoplasm.
rationales.b: It is not confined to mitochondria because several later reactions occur in the cytosol.
rationales.d: The nucleus is not one of the two main compartments of the urea cycle.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH11_Q002.takeaway: N-acetylglutamate is the obligatory allosteric activator of CPS I.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH11_Q002.displayText:
Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I (CPS I) catalyzes the rate-limiting mitochondrial step of the urea cycle. It requires N-acetylglutamate as an essential allosteric activator.

Loss of N-acetylglutamate therefore markedly reduces CPS I activity.

rationales.a: Alanine is not the obligatory allosteric activator of CPS I.
rationales.c: Ornithine participates in the urea cycle but does not activate CPS I allosterically.
rationales.d: Citrulline is a urea-cycle intermediate, not the CPS I activator.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH11_Q003.takeaway: The X-linked urea-cycle disorder is OTC deficiency, or hyperammonemia type II.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH11_Q003.displayText:
An X-linked recessive urea-cycle disorder points to ornithine transcarbamylase (OTC) deficiency, classically called hyperammonemia type II.

OTC deficiency causes hyperammonemia, low citrulline and excess carbamoyl phosphate that spills into pyrimidine synthesis, producing elevated urinary orotic acid.

rationales.a: Citrullinemia is caused by argininosuccinate synthetase deficiency and is not the classic X-linked disorder.
rationales.b: Hyperammonemia type I is caused by CPS I deficiency and is not X-linked.
rationales.d: Argininosuccinic aciduria is due to argininosuccinate lyase deficiency.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH11_Q004.takeaway: High glutamine with orotic-acid/uracil excess indicates OTC deficiency.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH11_Q004.displayText:
Hyperammonemia with high glutamine and excess uracil/orotic acid strongly suggests ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency. Accumulated mitochondrial carbamoyl phosphate enters cytosolic pyrimidine synthesis, increasing orotic acid and uracil.

This pattern distinguishes OTC deficiency from CPS I deficiency, which does not produce the same orotic-acid excess.

rationales.a: CPS I deficiency causes hyperammonemia but does not characteristically cause increased orotic acid from carbamoyl-phosphate overflow.
rationales.c: Argininosuccinate synthetase deficiency causes citrullinemia rather than the source-keyed orotic-acid pattern.
rationales.d: Argininosuccinate lyase deficiency causes argininosuccinic aciduria.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH11_Q005.displayText:
Argininosuccinate synthetase normally combines citrulline with aspartate to form argininosuccinate. Deficiency blocks this step and causes citrulline accumulation, producing citrullinemia.

The defect is part of the urea-cycle disorder spectrum.

rationales.a: Hyperargininemia is caused by arginase deficiency.
rationales.b: Argininosuccinic aciduria is caused by argininosuccinate lyase deficiency.
rationales.d: Hyperammonemia type I is caused by CPS I deficiency.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH11_Q006.takeaway: The two nitrogen atoms of urea come from free ammonia and aspartate.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH11_Q006.displayText:
Urea contains two nitrogen atoms. One is introduced as free ammonia during carbamoyl-phosphate formation, and the other is donated by aspartate during argininosuccinate formation.

This is the source of both nitrogens ultimately excreted as urea.

rationales.a: Glutamate is an important nitrogen carrier but is not directly the second nitrogen donor in urea.
rationales.c: Glutamine and arginine are not the two direct nitrogen sources of urea.
rationales.d: Arginine is the immediate precursor that is cleaved to release urea but does not directly supply the second nitrogen in the way stated here.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH11_Q007.takeaway: Fumarate is the metabolic link between the urea cycle and TCA cycle.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH11_Q007.displayText:
Argininosuccinate lyase splits argininosuccinate into arginine and fumarate. Fumarate can enter the TCA pathway through conversion to malate and then oxaloacetate.

This fumarate connection forms the aspartate–argininosuccinate shunt linking the urea and Krebs cycles.
emphasis: linking the urea and Krebs cycles

rationales.a: Arginine is a urea-cycle intermediate but is not the direct metabolic bridge into the TCA cycle.
rationales.b: Ornithine participates in the urea cycle but does not provide the TCA linkage asked here.
rationales.d: Oxaloacetate participates downstream after fumarate conversion, but fumarate is the source-keyed link generated directly by the urea cycle.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH11_Q009.takeaway: High argininosuccinate with low arginine indicates argininosuccinate lyase deficiency.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH11_Q009.displayText:
Argininosuccinate lyase converts argininosuccinate into arginine and fumarate. Deficiency therefore causes argininosuccinate accumulation with reduced arginine and produces argininosuccinic aciduria.

Affected neonates can develop severe hyperammonemia, neurologic deterioration and trichorrhexis nodosa.

rationales.a: Argininosuccinate synthetase deficiency causes citrullinemia rather than high argininosuccinate.
rationales.d: CPS I deficiency causes hyperammonemia type I and does not produce high argininosuccinate.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH11_Q010.takeaway: Hydrolysis in the urea cycle occurs when arginase cleaves arginine to urea and ornithine.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH11_Q010.displayText:
The hydrolytic step of the urea cycle is the arginase reaction. Arginine is hydrolyzed to produce urea and regenerate ornithine.

Arginase deficiency causes hyperargininemia.

rationales.b: Formation of argininosuccinate is an ATP-dependent condensation reaction, not hydrolysis.
rationales.c: Formation of citrulline is catalyzed by OTC and is not the hydrolytic step.
rationales.d: Cleavage of argininosuccinate is catalyzed by argininosuccinate lyase and is not the arginase hydrolysis reaction.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH11_Q011.takeaway: HHH syndrome is caused by a mitochondrial ornithine transporter defect.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH11_Q011.displayText:
Hyperammonemia, hyperornithinemia and homocitrullinuria define HHH syndrome. The defect is impaired mitochondrial ornithine transport, which disrupts normal urea-cycle function.

The characteristic triad directly points to an ornithine transporter defect.

rationales.a: Citrin defects cause a different mitochondrial transport disorder and do not match the HHH triad.
rationales.c: Carnitine acyl-transferase defects impair fatty-acid oxidation rather than producing HHH syndrome.
rationales.d: The source specifically keys the ornithine transporter defect option; 'ornithine permease' is not the accepted wording here.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH11_Q012.takeaway: Phenylbutyrate lowers ammonia by providing an alternate route for nitrogen excretion.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH11_Q012.displayText:
Phenylbutyrate acts as a nitrogen scavenger in urea-cycle disorders. It is converted to phenylacetate, which conjugates amino-acid nitrogen into a water-soluble product that can be excreted by the kidneys.

This provides an alternate route for nitrogen disposal and lowers ammonia.

rationales.a: Glutamate is a nitrogen carrier but is not the source-keyed ammonia-scavenging therapy.
rationales.c: Isoleucine is an amino acid and does not provide the alternate nitrogen-excretion pathway described.
rationales.d: L-carnitine is used in selected metabolic disorders but is not the source-keyed scavenger for urea-cycle hyperammonemia.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH11_Q013.takeaway: CPS II belongs to pyrimidine synthesis, not the urea cycle.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH11_Q013.displayText:
Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase II (CPS II) is a cytosolic enzyme of de novo pyrimidine synthesis. The urea cycle instead uses mitochondrial CPS I.

OTC, argininosuccinate lyase and arginase are genuine urea-cycle enzymes.

rationales.b: Ornithine transcarbamylase is a urea-cycle enzyme.
rationales.c: Argininosuccinate lyase is part of the urea cycle.
rationales.d: Arginase catalyzes the final urea-cycle step that releases urea.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH11_Q014.takeaway: CPS I catalyzes the rate-limiting mitochondrial step of the urea cycle.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH11_Q014.displayText:
Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I is a mitochondrial enzyme that uses free ammonia to generate carbamoyl phosphate in the first committed, rate-limiting step of the urea cycle.

CPS II is the cytosolic isoenzyme used in pyrimidine synthesis.

rationales.b: Purine synthesis does not use CPS I.
rationales.c: Pyrimidine synthesis uses cytosolic CPS II rather than mitochondrial CPS I.
rationales.d: The glucuronic pathway is unrelated to CPS I.
